Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the About page for a company that makes scheduling software for medical clinics. Around 250 words.

output:
We started Meridian because a friend who runs a three-doctor family practice spent four hours a week untangling double-booked slots by hand. That was 2021. Her front desk had a whiteboard, a paper calendar, and a scheduling tool built for restaurants.

Clinics book differently than everyone else. A follow-up needs the same doctor as last time. A new patient intake needs forty minutes, not fifteen. A no-show in an urgent-care slot costs more than one in a routine checkup, and a provider on maternity leave can't just vanish from the calendar without someone reassigning her patients first. We built Meridian around those constraints instead of bolting them onto generic booking software.

The product handles multi-provider calendars, insurance-aware intake forms, and waitlists that fill a cancelled slot automatically. It syncs with the major EHR systems clinics already run, so front-desk staff aren't re-entering the same patient twice. Clinics using it report shorter phone queues and fewer missed appointments, though the number that matters most to us is simpler: staff stop dreading Monday mornings.

We're a team of fourteen, split between Austin and remote, with three former clinic administrators on staff who test every feature against how their old front desks actually worked. No venture-backed growth targets forcing shortcuts, no enterprise sales cycle dictating the roadmap. We serve independent and small-group practices, the ones large hospital systems often ignore.

Meridian now runs scheduling for more than 600 clinics across 38 states. We're still adding features one clinic request at a time, the way we started.
